article.headline: Mexican redleg tarantula care guide
article.description: A detailed guide to keeping Brachypelma emilia: size, terrarium, substrate, temperature, humidity, feeding, hairs and moulting.

name: Mexican redleg tarantula
lead: A classic Mexican tarantula with black and red markings and a dark triangle on its carapace. One of the calmest species and an excellent first spider.
photoAlt: Mexican redleg tarantula (Brachypelma emilia) - NS Reptiles Novi Sad
intro: The Mexican redleg tarantula (Brachypelma emilia) comes from western Mexico. It is recognised by its black body, red-orange patches on the legs and a dark triangle on its light carapace. It is one of the calmest tarantulas: slow, rarely defensive, and females live for decades, which makes it an excellent first spider. To get started, we also offer a tarantula starter kit with an enclosure and substrate.

boxes.title: Origin and habitat
p: It comes from western Mexico (Sinaloa, Durango, Nayarit), from dry forests and scrubland, where it lives in burrows in the ground. All Brachypelma species are protected under CITES, so only buy legally captive-bred animals.

boxes.title: Size and appearance
p: A medium-sized tarantula: adult females reach a leg span of about 12-14 cm. The body is black, the legs have red-orange patches, and the light front part of the carapace carries a dark triangular marking.

boxes.title: Behaviour
p: One of the calmest tarantulas - it is slow and rarely shows aggression, and when frightened it usually just retreats into its hide. When it feels seriously threatened, it too flicks hairs from its abdomen.

boxes.title: Terrarium
p: This is a terrestrial species, so it needs a horizontal terrarium - floor space matters more than height. An enclosure with a floor of about 30×30 cm is enough for an adult. Leave only a few centimetres more than the spider's leg span above the substrate: a fall can rupture the abdomen and be fatal. The lid must close tightly, and ventilation should be both on the sides and on top. Spiderlings are kept in smaller containers, in proportion to their size.

boxes.title: Substrate
p: Provide 8-10 cm of substrate: coco peat or a mix of peat, fertiliser-free soil and a little sand. The substrate should be mostly dry, with one slightly moist corner.

boxes.title: Hide and decor
p: A half cork bark or a piece of bark as a hide, a shallow water dish and a few dry leaves or artificial plants are enough. Place heavier items on the bottom before adding substrate, so they cannot fall on the spider while it digs. Do not overcrowd the enclosure.

boxes.title: Temperature and light
p: Room temperature of about 22-27 °C suits it. If it gets colder in winter, put a heat mat on a side or back wall, never under the substrate - the spider escapes heat by digging down, so heating from below could overheat it. No special lighting or UVB is needed; avoid direct sunlight.

boxes.title: Humidity and water
p: It comes from drier areas, so humidity of about 50-65% suits it - too much moisture is bad for it. More important than humidity is a dish of clean water, which must always be in the enclosure.

boxes.title: Prey
p: It feeds on live insects: crickets, roaches (e.g. dubia), locusts and similar prey. Prey should not be larger than the spider's abdomen. Do not feed wild-caught insects, as they may carry parasites and pesticides.

boxes.title: Feeding frequency
p: Adults need food once a week or less, spiderlings twice a week with smaller prey. Remove prey that is not eaten within a day. It is normal for a tarantula to refuse food for weeks before a moult - do not offer food then.

boxes.title: Urticating hairs
p: Like other tarantulas from the Americas, it has urticating hairs on the abdomen that it flicks off with its legs when threatened. On the skin they cause itching and redness, and in the eyes serious irritation. Keep your face away when working in the enclosure and wash your hands afterwards. This species flicks hairs less often than most related species, but it does have them.

boxes.title: Venom
p: The venom of this species is not dangerous to a healthy person - a bite is comparable to a bee or wasp sting: pain, redness and swelling that pass. As with a bee sting, an allergic reaction is possible; if breathing becomes difficult or swelling spreads, seek medical help immediately.

boxes.title: Handling
p: We do not recommend handling. A fall from just a few dozen centimetres can be fatal for a tarantula, and a frightened spider may bite or flick hairs. To move it, guide the spider into a clear container and cover it with a piece of card. Keep the enclosure out of reach of children and pets.

boxes.title: Growth and lifespan
p: It grows slowly - it takes several years to reach adult size. Females can live 20-30 years, males much less.

boxes.title: Moulting
p: A tarantula grows by moulting. Before a moult it stops eating and its abdomen darkens. It usually moults lying on its back - this is normal and not a sign of death, so do not touch it. After the moult wait at least a week before feeding, until the new exoskeleton and fangs harden. No live prey may be left in the enclosure at that time.

boxes.title: Possible problems
p: The biggest risks are falls, dehydration and live prey left in during a moult. A spider pulling its legs under its body is a serious sign - check that it has water and contact an experienced breeder or an exotic animal vet. Mould and mites appear in an overly wet, poorly ventilated enclosure with food leftovers.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about the mexican redleg tarantula

items.q: Is the mexican redleg tarantula venomous?
items.a: It is not dangerous to a healthy person - a bite is similar to a bee sting. The bigger nuisance is the urticating hairs from the abdomen, which irritate the skin and eyes.

items.q: How big does the mexican redleg tarantula get?
items.a: Adult females reach a leg span of about 12-14 cm.

items.q: How long does the mexican redleg tarantula live?
items.a: Females can live 20-30 years, males much less.

items.q: What does the mexican redleg tarantula eat?
items.a: Live insects of the right size - crickets, roaches and locusts. Adults only need feeding once a week or less.

items.q: Is the mexican redleg tarantula good for beginners?
items.a: Yes, it is one of the best species for a first spider - calm, slow, undemanding and long-lived.

items.q: Can you handle a mexican redleg tarantula?
items.a: We do not recommend it. A fall can be fatal for the spider, and a frightened tarantula may bite or flick irritating hairs. Use a container to move it.
